summary: German attacks can still penetrate a Soviet line, but the army group cannot sustain their gains. The final attempts around Moscow and Tula reveal why renewed movement no longer offers a decision.
body:
The offensive that could still hurt

On 2 December 1941, the German offensive could still inflict a dangerous local reverse. The previous day, the 258th Infantry Division had broken through the Soviet line south of the Moscow–Smolensk highway. Northeast of Tula, Guderian's Second Panzer Army was attempting another westward movement to cut off the city. These were real operations, undertaken by formations that retained weapons, organisation, and the ability to attack. They were also being conducted within an army group whose commander had just warned that it lacked the strength to complete the encirclement of Moscow. The contradiction defines this stage of the campaign.[1]

Bock's predicament was that a real success could still invite an unattainable conclusion. The 258th Division had opened a breach, but his army group had no substantial fresh force waiting to turn it into a decisive advance. Hoepner and Reinhardt were already engaged on the northern approaches, while Guderian was again trying to close a ring around Tula. Each command needed help from another command that was itself struggling. German troops retained the ability to attack a position; the army group was losing the ability to connect those attacks into the operation for which they had been ordered.[1]

This study follows the last German attacks from the local openings of 1–2 December through the decisions to stop them on the 3rd and 4th. It ends before the wider Soviet counteroffensive examined in the concluding study. That short interval matters because German failure was not yet experienced as a quiet front awaiting a Soviet attack. Infantry penetrated a defensive line, Guderian attempted to close Tula’s encirclement and Soviet formations counterattacked while others were still arriving. Commanders were deciding whether to continue in the midst of actions that could still endanger the defence of Moscow.[1]

A breakthrough without an exploitation

The 258th Infantry Division's attack mattered because it occurred in Fourth Army's sector, where progress had been too slow to support the northern pincer as Bock desired. The Soviet line south of the principal western highway was penetrated on 1 December. For a short time, that success offered the possibility that the centre of the German operation might move again while the panzer groups continued pressing farther north. Bock's assessments on 2 December reflected the resulting uncertainty: he could still tell commanders that the opponent was close to breaking while warning Halder later that prospects were deteriorating.[1]

By the afternoon of 3 December, the 258th Division was fighting its way back west out of an encirclement. The breach had exposed the advancing force without producing a corresponding collapse on its flanks. Bock had hoped that success in Fourth Army's sector would help revive the wider attack; instead, the division needed to extricate itself. That reversal gives a precise limit to the achievement of the 1st. The Soviet line had been penetrated, and the danger on 2 December was real, but the German command had failed to create the conditions in which its successful infantry could remain forward and continue.[1]

Fourth Army's commander, Günther von Kluge, later became a convenient figure in explanations that attributed failure to reluctance or insufficient offensive spirit. David Stahel rejects the idea that Kluge possessed an unused force capable of turning the campaign into victory. In the accessible opening of his chapter on the final approaches, he emphasises the weakness of Fourth Army's right wing and the exhaustion of the panzer groups. This is a scholarly interpretation, but it accords with the operational record of limited advances, formations reduced by losses, and attacks that could not be sustained.[2][1]

Kluge proposed abandoning Fourth Army's attack on the morning of 3 December because it would not get through to Moscow. Bock preferred to wait another two or three days to see whether Reinhardt's movement from the north could change the position. By that afternoon, the 258th Division was withdrawing from its predicament and Fourth Panzer Group was reporting its offensive strength largely exhausted. Fourth Army went over to the defensive on the 4th. The sequence shows the different judgements operating within the same command: Kluge assessed his immediate attack, while Bock kept looking for another formation whose success might make it worthwhile to persist.[1]

The two pincers no longer converge

In the north, Third Panzer Group's turn south from the canal had not produced a decisive combination with Fourth Panzer Group. Reinhardt's formations remained engaged around Yakhroma and threatened along their extended northern side. Hoepner's troops were struggling around Krasnaya Polyana and farther south, with Soviet positions requiring direct attacks. The operational picture therefore differed from the geometric promise of two mobile formations curving around a capital. They were fighting separate, increasingly costly battles while trying to preserve their connection to neighbouring commands.[1]

The Soviet First Shock Army was no longer merely a prospective reinforcement. Its elements had made contact with the Germans late in November, and on 2 December Kuznetsov received instructions for the Zakharov group to attack toward Dednevo and Fedorovka, with Klin as a longer-term direction. The immediate objectives were local. The group included parts of three divisions and a tank brigade that had served as a rearguard around Klin and were now pinned west of the canal. The order combined relief of an immediate tactical situation with the possibility of a wider advance if the fighting developed favourably.[1]

South of Moscow, Guderian's operation remained entangled with Tula. The city had not fallen, and bypassing it had created an extended bulge without eliminating the defenders. The westward hook attempted on 2 December sought to close the problem by cutting off Tula and potentially releasing pressure on Fourth Army's right wing. Its strategic value depended on more than reaching another point on the perimeter. The Germans had to maintain the connection around the city while Soviet forces threatened their eastern side and the routes toward Kashira.[1]

The Soviet response in the southern sector had become more substantial. Pavel Belov's cavalry grouping, now the First Guards Cavalry Corps, operated with supporting rifle and armoured forces around the Kashira approaches. The Fiftieth Army continued defending Tula, while the Tenth Army was moving toward the Oka sector farther east. These formations were not all available in the same condition or at the same moment. Together, however, they made it harder for Guderian to treat the area beyond his leading units as empty space through which an encirclement could be completed.[1]

Guderian's own account follows the southern attack into a particularly revealing result on 3 December. Fourth Panzer Division damaged the Tula–Moscow railway and reached the Serpukhov–Tula road, then stopped with its troops exhausted and fuel expended. Here the Germans had actually reached and disrupted a communication, unlike the failed late-November patrols toward the Ryazan–Kolomna railway. Yet the success still did not close the ring around Tula. It created a narrow projection needing support from troops whose own advance was faltering. The achievement was substantial enough to threaten the defenders and insufficient to remove their ability to resist.[3]

Strength on paper and strength in the line

German losses had become a problem of replacement as well as casualties. Stahel reports 743,112 casualties in the eastern campaign by 26 November, excluding men removed through sickness. The figure covers the campaign, not Moscow alone, and combines categories that must not be read as deaths. His public extract also describes divisions redistributing their surviving men because replacements were inadequate. These measures could keep formations in existence without restoring the strength needed for their assigned fronts. The figures support an assessment of cumulative depletion; they cannot tell us the number of riflemen available to a particular company on 2 December.[4]

Twenty men in a company

Stahel cites a German non-commissioned officer's letter home of 21 November describing a company reduced to twenty men as early as October. The formation later redistributed personnel by dissolving a battalion in each regiment. This was one man's account, not a strength return for every German company. It nevertheless shows how reorganisation could improve the apparent condition of surviving units without bringing fresh soldiers into the division. The men still present inherited the duties of the formations that disappeared.[4]

The remaining administrative structure could hide the loss of fighting capacity. Headquarters still issued orders, artillery still required supply and rear services still carried out their tasks even when a division’s infantry had shrunk drastically. Consolidating battalions helped commanders organise the men who remained; it did not recreate the men lost. The resulting formations could still inflict a local defeat, as the 258th Division demonstrated. Their difficulty was sustaining the advance, protecting its sides and retaining a reserve after making that effort. The count of divisional headquarters was consequently a poor guide to how many further attacks Bock could demand.[1][5]

North of Tula, this weakness took the form of troops and vehicles stranded near an objective they had reached but could not exploit. Guderian records Soviet forces on both sides of the German wedge toward the Serpukhov road on 4 December. Third Panzer Division fought east of Tula with little progress, while Forty-Third Corps still had to close the gap from the west. Fourth Panzer Division's position could not be secured merely by keeping its remaining tanks there. It depended on infantry and neighbouring formations reaching the threatened ground before Soviet attacks cut the narrow connection back to the army.[3]

Supporting infantry was still on the road. Guderian records the 296th Infantry Division reaching the Yasnaya Polyana area on 4 December but being unable to attack that day. It was supposed to help close Tula from the south and west. Its delay left the advanced troops without the connection their position required. This is a named instance of the failure of coordination, rather than a general complaint about winter. The division existed, had an assignment and was moving toward it. None of those facts put its infantry beside Fourth Panzer Division at the moment when the forward force needed support.[3]

Cold worsened these weaknesses, but the sequence must remain clear. The final offensive had lost momentum through fighting, attrition, and supply strain before the most severe early-December conditions described in German reports. Frozen ground had earlier helped vehicles move after the mud. Later cold and snow imposed different difficulties, including starting engines, handling weapons, sheltering troops, and evacuating wounded men. Weather did not act as a single event that suddenly converted a victorious army into a defeated one. Its effects accumulated within an already deteriorating military situation.[1]

The Soviet armies were also short of the means to exploit movement. Golikov’s Tenth Army travelled largely by rail and on foot; Kuznetsov’s First Shock Army lacked the intended complement of armour and transport. These deficiencies shaped what they could attempt even as German capacity declined. Soviet advantage did not rest on immunity to cold or on limitless, perfectly equipped reserves. It rested on preserving enough forces and introducing others where the German army could no longer meet every threat. Their arrival changed the balance, but their condition imposed limits on the counteroffensive being prepared.[1]

Reserves that had to arrive

The Tenth Army provides a particularly clear example of the difference between formation and availability. Under Filipp Golikov, it had been assembling around Syzran on the Volga. The U.S. Army history describes seven reserve rifle divisions and approximately one hundred thousand troops, while emphasising the shortage of motor vehicles. After receiving marching orders on 24 November, the army had to cover more than three hundred miles by rail and on foot. Those figures describe an army in movement, not one hundred thousand fully equipped men already standing in a line east of Tula.[1]

The railway Guderian had tried to cut in November had not been securely interdicted. His patrols failed to reach the Ryazan–Kolomna objective, while Golikov’s army continued its long movement toward the Oka sector. That connection gives the earlier patrol failure a significance beyond an unsuccessful raid. German leading troops had reached deep into Soviet territory without closing every approach by which the defender could reinforce. Golikov still faced serious transport shortages, so arrival remained uneven. Yet his movement was possible. The German army had created a vulnerable eastern flank without eliminating the routes that could bring an opponent against it.[1][3]

Stalin retained control over the commitment of additional reserve armies east of Moscow. Some were held for defence if the situation worsened, or for developing a counteroffensive if that became possible. This was a significant restraint compared with earlier moments when new forces had been committed rapidly into unsuccessful attacks. It did not mean the Soviet leadership possessed certainty about the outcome. The reserves were insurance against a continuing danger as well as a means of changing the battle. Their allocation reflected the need to preserve both possibilities.[1]

The Soviet memoirs emphasise different reasons for acting. Zhukov presents a German force severely depleted by the defence; Vasilevsky stresses that active operations were urgently needed to halt a continuing danger. The U.S. Army history juxtaposes those accounts. Neither retrospective emphasis should be treated as the exact mental state of every commander on 2 December. They illuminate a real strategic tension: the Germans were weakening, but waiting for them to stop and entrench might squander the opportunity to remove the threat. The counteroffensive was being prepared to exploit exhaustion while preventing another dangerous local success.[1]

The transfer of authority on 29 November was a concrete step in turning reserves into a coordinated response. After Zhukov assured Stalin that major fresh German forces were unlikely to enter the battle immediately, Stalin placed the First Shock, Twentieth, and Tenth armies under Zhukov’s control for a counterattack. This did not complete their assembly or determine the outcome of every engagement. It gave the front commander responsibility for combining their actions with those of the armies already fighting around Moscow. The decision also rested on an assessment of German capacity: Soviet leaders were judging how much risk they could accept while moving from immediate containment toward a broader effort to recover the initiative.[1]

The capital behind the positions

Moscow's defence had mobilised civilians as well as armies. During the October crisis, civilians, many of them women, had worked on defensive lines, while militia formations were organised for the city's protection. Those preparations remained part of the landscape the Germans were now approaching. Fieldworks did not defend themselves, but they could give troops cover, obstruct vehicles, and make an attacker deploy under fire. Civilian labour had therefore contributed to the time and effort required of the German formations in late November and early December.[5][1]

The civilian effort was carried out under emergency government. Moscow remained subject to the state of siege introduced in October, while military and administrative authorities directed labour, transport and defence. That coercive setting is part of the achievement, not a reason to deny that the city continued functioning. Factories and families had been displaced; defensive work competed with ordinary necessities; the surviving systems still had to feed people and move forces. The capital’s endurance depended on organised work amid deprivation, rather than on a population acting with a single uncomplicated emotion.[5][6]

The misleading view from a map

Stahel draws attention to the impression created by headquarters maps at a scale of one to a million: German panzer groups appeared poised close to Moscow. At that scale, the distance remaining could look modest while the weakness of the formations was invisible. A position symbol did not show how many men were fit, how many vehicles would start, or how much ammunition could be delivered. The geographic proximity was real; the implication of an imminent decisive blow was an interpretation that required evidence the map could not supply.[2]

At the level of an army group, proximity had become a deceptive measure of success. A force close to Moscow might still need to defeat another defensive position, bring up supporting infantry and preserve a road behind it. Bock’s messages reveal awareness of those requirements: he warned that his army group could not encircle the city while the high command continued discussing much farther objectives. His complaint concerned the mismatch between resources and orders. It did not mean that every unit had stopped fighting, or that the defenders could safely disregard the ground the Germans had already reached.[2][1]

The economic strain extended far beyond the visible front. Evacuation removed plant and workers from the invader’s reach while interrupting production and placing new demands on receiving regions. Harrison describes a choice with costs on either side: moving too early could sacrifice output; moving too late could lose the enterprise. In November and December, the Red Army was still fighting through the resulting trough in industrial supply. The later recovery cannot explain its survival as if the restored factories had already delivered their full output. What mattered immediately was maintaining enough production, stocks and transport to sustain the armies during that disruption.[6]

Readiness on the two sides was uneven in different ways. German formations had equipment they could no longer move reliably and fronts they lacked the infantry to hold comfortably. New Soviet armies supplied additional manpower but often lacked transport and supporting weapons. The shift in advantage came from how those unequal deficiencies met in battle. Another Soviet brigade at a threatened point might be sufficient to stop a depleted German division even though it was insufficient for a sustained pursuit. That limited effectiveness helps explain both the collapse of the German offensive and the difficult opening of the Soviet response.[1]

Choosing how to stop

By 3 December, Bock was explaining his persistence partly through fear of the alternative. Remaining on the offensive seemed preferable to adopting a defensive posture with weakened troops in exposed positions. That argument captures a trap created by the advance itself. The army had moved into ground it could not comfortably hold, yet withdrawing or preparing a coherent defence required decisions that would acknowledge the failure of its immediate aims. Continuing to attack postponed that acknowledgement while consuming the resources needed for the transition.[1]

The Soviet command sought to strike during precisely that transition, before the Germans could regroup and establish a more secure winter line. Preparation for the broader counteroffensive intensified over the following days. Its opening would be staggered, with attacks on 5 December and wider operations on 6 December. Those developments belong to the concluding Phase V study. On 2 December, the immediate picture remained one of overlapping attempts: German local attacks seeking to revive a failing offensive, and Soviet actions intended to remove the remaining threat and seize the initiative.[1]

By 4 December, Fourth Army had gone over to the defensive. Hoepner reported that he could not advance until Reinhardt came abreast; Reinhardt faced additional Soviet pressure; Guderian was still trying to complete his operation around Tula. Bock’s army group had failed to connect its local attacks into the envelopment it sought. The danger to Moscow was still being contested, but Germany no longer had a credible means of obtaining the quick decision promised by its campaign. The next day would bring both another German attempt and the opening of Konev’s counteroffensive. The initiative was changing through battle, not through a single declaration that the offensive was over.[1]

chronologyNotes: Do not turn disputed reconnaissance or closest-approach claims into verified occupation.

sourceMethod: Numbered notes connect the prose to specific inspected passages. The U.S. Army campaign history is a retrospective synthesis, assessed alongside Soviet documentary transcriptions, institutional accounts and scholarship. Guderian’s and German signals officers’ postwar explanations are attributed; their criticisms of higher command are not independent proof of their own conduct. Public Cambridge extracts, edited diary selections and catalogue-only evidence are identified in the locators. Russian and German material is paraphrased in English; uninspected archival originals are not claimed as consulted. Orders, reported implementation and independently established outcomes remain distinct. Operational analysis is Ostkrieg’s interpretation of the cited evidence. This local editorial revision does not validate or update the companion maps or their cached passages.
